title: ESAU MARRIED TWO HITTITE WOMEN—And They Made Life Bitter for His Parents
paragraphs:
ESAU MARRIED TWO HITTITE WOMEN—And They Made Life Bitter for His Parents
Genesis records the wedding in one sentence. Then, in the next, Scripture tells us what happened inside the home: “bitterness of spirit.” And buried inside those two verses is a warning for every person who thinks a private decision can never wound the people who love them.
There are weddings where parents cry because they are happy.
And then there are tears nobody photographs.
No one posts them.
No one sees the mother lying awake afterward.
No one hears the father wondering where things changed.
No one sees what happens when somebody you raised, prayed over, protected, corrected, forgave, and loved becomes old enough to make decisions you can no longer make for them.
Genesis gives us one of those moments.
Almost brutally.
No long explanation.
No dramatic speech.
Just two verses.
“When Esau was forty years old, he took to wife Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath daughter of Elon the Hittite…”
Then comes the sentence that changes the emotional temperature of the entire scene:
“וַתִּהְיֶיןָ מֹרַת רוּחַ לְיִצְחָק וּלְרִבְקָה”
Vattihyena morat ruaḥ le-Yitzḥaq u-le-Rivqah.
Literally, the Hebrew carries the sense that they became “bitterness of spirit” to Isaac and Rebekah.
Genesis 26:34–35.
Not merely an inconvenience.
Not simply an awkward disagreement between generations.
Bitterness of spirit.
Imagine those words inside a home.
Esau was forty years old.
That detail matters.
This was not a child who did not know better.
This was a grown man making grown decisions.
And that may be exactly where this passage begins hurting some of us.
Because eventually your children grow beyond the reach of your hands.
You can teach them.
You can warn them.
You can pray for them.
You can show them truth.
You can tell them what God has done in your family.
But there comes a day when they make choices while you stand close enough to watch and too far away to choose for them.
Some parents reading this know that pain.
Your son is alive, but you barely recognize the direction of his life.
Your daughter still calls you “Mom,” but she no longer wants the God you taught her to love.
Maybe someone you raised has walked into a relationship that is pulling them farther from Christ.
Maybe you watched somebody you love trade conviction for companionship.
Maybe your family photographs still look beautiful while something underneath them is breaking.
And perhaps nobody knows.
You smile at church.
You answer, “We’re doing fine.”
You change the subject when somebody asks about your children.
Then you go home carrying what Genesis calls מֹרַת רוּחַ — morat ruaḥ.
Bitterness of spirit.
But we need to be careful here.
Genesis 26 is not giving Christians permission to despise people because of ethnicity, nationality, family background, or because they are “outsiders.”
That would badly mishandle the passage.
The issue belongs to the unfolding covenant story.

Abraham had previously been deeply concerned that Isaac not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Later, Rebekah herself would say concerning Esau’s Hittite wives, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth” (Genesis 27:46). And Genesis 28 tells us that Esau eventually recognized that “the daughters of Canaan pleased not Isaac his father.”
Something deeper than parental preference was happening.
Esau was living inside a family carrying covenant promises from God while repeatedly showing how little spiritual inheritance seemed to weigh upon him.
And we had already seen it.
Before these marriages, Esau came home exhausted.
Jacob had food.
Esau had a birthright.
One satisfied his stomach for a few hours.
The other represented inheritance, privilege, responsibility, and covenant significance.
And Esau said, essentially, What good is the birthright to me if I am about to die?
He traded what was sacred for what was immediate.
Genesis 25 ends that episode with terrifying simplicity:
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
That is the shadow standing behind Genesis 26.
The marriages did not suddenly create Esau’s spiritual problem.
They revealed something that had already been growing.
And that is where this ancient story walks straight into our lives.
Because most spiritual disasters do not begin on the day everybody notices them.
They begin quietly.
A compromise nobody confronts.
A conviction repeatedly ignored.
A prayer life slowly abandoned.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, but loneliness makes you afraid to let go.
A habit you keep defending.
A resentment you keep feeding.
A secret browser history.
A conversation you would immediately delete if your spouse picked up your phone.
A church attendance that remains while your hunger for God disappears.
Nobody wakes up one morning planning to become spiritually cold.
We drift there through decisions.
One appetite.
One justification.
One compromise.
One “just this once.”
One “God understands.”
One “everybody does it.”
One “I can stop whenever I want.”
Until something that once disturbed your conscience becomes normal.
That is one of the frightening things about Esau.
He does not appear to wake up every morning announcing war against God.
He simply keeps choosing what is immediately desirable without adequately treasuring what is spiritually weighty.
And Scripture later remembers him for it.
Hebrews 12 warns believers not to become “profane” like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright.
Think about that.
One meal.
The food disappeared.
The decision remained.
Somebody reading this needs that sentence.
The appetite will pass. The consequences may remain.
That relationship feels impossible to surrender right now.
That temptation feels unbearable right now.
That anger feels justified right now.
That secret sin feels comforting right now.
That compromise feels profitable right now.
But “right now” is a dangerous god.
Esau teaches us what happens when immediate appetite becomes more authoritative than eternal truth.
And before we point at him too confidently, we should look in the mirror.
How many times have we done our own version of the same thing?
We knew what Scripture said.
But we wanted something.
We knew what obedience required.
But obedience was expensive.
We knew the Holy Spirit was convicting us.
But compromise felt easier.
So we chose the bowl.
Different bowl.
Same temptation.
And sometimes other people end up tasting the bitterness of decisions they never made.
Isaac and Rebekah did.
That is another uncomfortable truth hidden inside Genesis 26.
Sin loves telling us:
“This is my life. My decision. It affects nobody but me.”
Scripture repeatedly destroys that illusion.
Our choices ripple.
A father's hidden addiction can eventually enter the emotional atmosphere of his home.
A mother's bitterness can shape how her children understand forgiveness.
A spouse's secret betrayal can fracture somebody else's ability to trust.
A young person's rebellion can leave praying parents awake at two in the morning.
And parents can wound children too.
This passage must never become ammunition for parents who want to control adult sons and daughters under the banner of “honoring God.”
Isaac and Rebekah themselves were not a flawless family.
Keep reading Genesis.
Favoritism entered that house.
Isaac favored Esau.
Rebekah favored Jacob.
Deception followed.
Manipulation followed.
Heartbreak followed.
The Bible does not airbrush its families.
That is one reason Scripture feels so painfully real.
God does not give us polished families pretending everything is fine.
He gives us tents full of tension.
Parents with weaknesses.
Children making destructive decisions.
Brothers fighting.
Spouses grieving.
People deceiving one another.
People running away.
People carrying consequences.
And somehow…
God keeps writing.
That may be the most beautiful thing in the entire story.
Because if Genesis were only about human faithfulness, the story would collapse almost immediately.
Abraham failed.
Isaac failed.
Rebekah failed.
Jacob failed spectacularly.
Esau made devastating choices.
The family became messy enough that if their story happened today, people would probably argue about them endlessly in comment sections.
Yet the covenant promise did not survive because this family was impressive.
It survived because God is faithful.
And eventually, generations later, from the covenant line would come Jesus Christ.
That is where this story must ultimately take us.
Not merely:
“Choose better relationships.”
Not merely:
“Listen to your parents.”
Not merely:
“Don't become like Esau.”
Those lessons can have their place.
But Christianity is not a self-improvement program for people trying harder not to embarrass their families.
The Gospel goes much deeper.
Because the deepest problem is not that Esau once made terrible decisions.
The deeper problem is that something of Esau lives inside every sinner.
We have all preferred lesser things to God.
We have all exchanged holiness for appetite in one form or another.
We have all sinned.
We have all wounded others.
We have all chosen things we later wished we could unchoose.
And some of you are reading this article carrying exactly that kind of regret.
You are not Isaac or Rebekah in this story.
You feel like Esau.
You were the one who made life bitter.
You were the child who rebelled.
You were the spouse who betrayed.
You were the parent who failed.
You were the person who ignored every warning until the consequences finally arrived.
And now you would give almost anything to return to the moment before everything changed.
Listen carefully.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday did to you.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Grace is not pretending sin never mattered.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin mattered so much that our reconciliation with God required a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve sinners.
He came to save them.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore sin for sinners.
The One who never traded righteousness for appetite carried the judgment deserved by people who have.
The One perfectly obedient to the Father died for the disobedient.
And He rose again.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you home.
You do not have to keep defending the thing destroying you.
You do not have to rename darkness so you can continue living inside it.
You do not have to pretend the bitterness isn't bitter.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can come to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That promise in 1 John 1:9 is not sentimental optimism.
It rests on Jesus.
Maybe you have become Esau in somebody else's story.
Then repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Now.
Call the person you wounded if reconciliation is appropriate and safe.
Tell the truth.
Stop hiding.
Bring the secret into the light.
Ask forgiveness without demanding that the wounded person immediately trust you again.
Accept that repentance may require restitution, changed behavior, boundaries, accountability, patience, and time.
Grace is free.
Transformation will cost your pride.
And maybe you are Isaac or Rebekah.
You are watching someone you love make decisions that hurt.
Then hear this too:
You cannot be their Holy Spirit.
You cannot repent for them.
You cannot force regeneration.
You can speak truth.
You can establish wise boundaries.
You can refuse to finance destruction.
You can refuse to call evil good simply to keep the peace.
But you can also keep praying.
Keep loving without enabling.
Keep your heart from becoming poisoned by the bitterness of what happened.
Because there is another danger here.
Someone else's rebellion can become your bitterness.
And suddenly their sin has wounded your heart twice.
Once through what they did.
Then again through what you allowed their decision to turn you into.
Give that bitterness to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again if necessary.
Some prayers are prayed with confidence.
Others come out as tears.
God hears both.
And please remember something Genesis itself teaches repeatedly:
God can still be working in a family that looks completely broken.
You may be looking at chapter 26 while God already knows chapter 33.
You may be staring at the scandal while God is still writing.
That does not guarantee every relationship will be restored exactly as we want it in this life.
The Bible never promises that.
But it does mean human failure does not dethrone God.
Your child's rebellion is not stronger than God.
Your past is not stronger than Christ's blood.
Your shame is not stronger than grace.
Your family history is not sovereign.
Jesus is.
Maybe that is why you found this today.
Not so you could criticize Esau.
But so Esau's story could expose something in you.
What are you trading?
What temporary appetite has become more precious than obedience?
What relationship are you protecting even though it is pulling you farther from Christ?
What secret are you defending?
Whose heart is becoming bitter because you refuse to repent?
Or whose choices have made your spirit bitter?
Sit with them.
Because sometimes the most dangerous sentence a Christian can say is:
“It's not that serious.”
Esau probably wanted dinner.
He could not see Hebrews 12 being written centuries later.
You cannot see every consequence attached to today's compromise either.
So choose Christ.
Not because obedience purchases His love.
Because in Christ you have encountered a love worth obeying.
Choose the Savior over the appetite.
Choose truth over secrecy.
Choose repentance over reputation.
Choose holiness over the thing you keep telling yourself you cannot live without.
And if you have already failed…
Come anyway.
Come ashamed.
Come trembling.
Come with consequences behind you.
Come with the smell of yesterday still on your clothes.
Come with nothing impressive to show God.
Just come to Jesus.
The Gospel was never good news because good people finally became perfect.
It is good news because a perfect Savior came looking for sinners.
This is Gospel Warrior.
And if something inside you was exposed while reading this, don't reduce this moment to another piece of content you consumed and forgot.
You do not need to explain everything publicly. God knows the details. But sometimes one honest sentence is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And look through those comments.
Somebody there may need encouragement.
Pray for them.
Remind them of Christ.
Let this become more than content. Let believers carry one another's burdens.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone who may desperately need it tonight.
Someone may be hiding a compromise.
Someone may be a parent crying over a child.
Someone may believe their scandal has placed them beyond grace.
Let them hear about Jesus.

Supporting Gospel ministry does not make God love you more, and it should never replace faithful giving, serving, or involvement in a biblical local church. But when believers voluntarily support sound Christian work, they help make more Gospel-centered resources possible.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Jesus is the One sinners need.
So share the article if it can reach somebody.
But above everything…
Follow Jesus.
Esau's story leaves us with bitterness in a family's home.
The Gospel takes us somewhere Esau could never have imagined.
To a cross.
To an empty tomb.
To sinners being forgiven.
To rebels becoming sons and daughters.
To shame losing its final word.
To people discovering that the worst chapter they wrote does not have to become the final chapter of their lives.
Because when Jesus enters the story, repentance can replace rebellion.
Grace can meet guilt.
Forgiveness can confront failure.
Redemption can rise out of wreckage.
And scars that once screamed only of what happened can someday testify to what Christ has done.
Maybe the bitter chapter is real—but it still doesn't get to write the ending.
